en: Introduction: Homage to the illustrious Hevajra.

I pay homage to the glorious Lord Heruka, who is filled with the mass of bliss, whose nature is the absence of intrinsic being, who is peaceful, equal to space, supreme, all-pervading, inseparable from emptiness, and abides within the womb of Nairātmyā;
who is formless, the four joys, who has reached the state of Nirvāṇa, who is free from defilement, pure, and who has conquered hatred—I bow to the Lord of Ḍākinīs, the Master of the Skull-Family.
I pay homage to the Lord Heruka, whose body is united with Nairātmyā;
I shall now explain his sādhana in accordance with the Root Tantra.

Now, having extracted from that which is stated in the *Śrīmad-Hevajra-Ḍākinījāla-mahātantrarāja*, the noble Saroruha-pāda—having concealed it for the sake of protecting the lineage and the instructions (*āmnāya-yoga-deśa*) from being lost, and seeing beings possessed of false pride, and out of fear of the *Ḍākinījāla*—has spoken this *Abhisamaya*. If, at the time when some slight "heat" (*ūṣma*) has been attained, for the purpose of clarifying the *Abhisamaya*, I—who am known by the name Bhadra, the grandson’s son of Saroruha-pāda, and who was requested by Kodālī—speak this *Dveṣavajra-sādhana* by the command of Vajraḍākinī; and likewise, having seen, heard, and realized what is stated in the Root Tantra, I speak it for the sake of those seekers who desire [liberation] through the *Śrīmad-Hevajra-Ḍākinījāla-mahātantrarāja*.

Now, first of all, as for the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*): the mantra-practitioner, having propitiated the guru through the sequential stages beginning with service (*ārādhana*), and having correctly received the instructions of the oral tradition (*āmnāya*) from the guru, should practice in secret until some degree of attainment (*lābha*) occurs. Once that has occurred—having generated the wisdom (*prajñā*) as described, either by his own power or by means of a sign—the yogi should go to a cremation ground, a forest, or a wilderness until the attainment of Mahāmudrā occurs.

This meditation should be practiced through secret yoga. Having sat in a comfortable posture, the mantra-practitioner visualizes the sun at his own heart by means of the syllable *repha*. Above that, he beholds a blue-colored *hūṃ* syllable emitting five rays of light. Having expanded those rays into the sky and illuminated infinite world-systems, he recites "This is Śrī Heruka," thereby inviting the mandala of his chosen deity, as well as the gurus, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others, and contemplates them before him. Having offered water for the feet (*argha-pādya*) and other honors, and having worshipped them with flowers, incense, and so forth, he then [visualizes] his chosen deity in front of him.
Gaurī holds a deer-marked [moon], Caurī a vessel for the sun,
Vetālī has water in her hand, and Ghasmarī holds medicine.
Pukkasi should hold a club, and Śabarī should be the bearer of nectar;
Caṇḍālī should play the hand-drum, and Ḍombī should display an embrace.
Having first worshipped with these [offerings] and having meditated upon the Blessed One whose body radiates and reabsorbs [light], one should perform the sevenfold unsurpassed worship before him.

Whatever sinful karma I have committed by being deceived by the whirlpools of birth throughout beginningless saṃsāra, wherever I was reborn—I confess all of that before the Blessed One so that it may never be done again. Furthermore, whatever merit has been performed, caused to be performed, or approved by others, whether in this life or in other births throughout saṃsāra, I rejoice in that merit of sentient beings. I also dedicate all of that toward my own unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, for the sake of causing sentient beings to generate the mind of awakening (bodhicitta). Having gone for refuge to the Buddha—the all-pervading great wisdom, the Vajra of the syllable *He*—to the Dharma as taught in the tantras, mantras, and so forth by him, and to the Saṅgha, the assembly of goddesses residing in that mandala; and having thought, "O Blessed One, please attend to me, so that I may attain the inexhaustible fruit," one should generate the mind of awakening. Thereafter, for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings, one should fix the mind upon emptiness endowed with the supreme of all aspects; this is the taking of the path. Then, having personally given oneself as a gift to those [beings], one should subsequently begin the practice of the means of achievement (*sādhana*).

Thereafter, first one should cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward all sentient beings as if they were the affection felt for an only son. In the second [moment], one cultivates compassion (*karuṇā*) toward those in the miserable states of existence, like a great ocean. In the third, having generated the Great Resolve (*mahacitta*), one thinks, "I must establish them all in perfect awakening," and realizing oneself as a perfected being in the form of Heruka, one laughs; this is sympathetic joy (*muditā*). In the fourth, there is equanimity (*upekṣā*), in which there is no grasping toward fame or infamy, gain or loss, pleasure or pain, praise or blame.

Thus, at the conclusion of the cultivation of the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), one should visualize oneself overcome by death. By means of the yoga of the *jñānālokavajra-samādhi*, having brought about the disappearance of the ordinary body, one should then instantly perceive the Lord Sahajanātha—extremely peaceful, possessing the thirty-two major marks and adorned with the eighty minor characteristics, seated in the vajra posture upon a corpse resting on a moon disc, illuminating infinite world-realms, his two arms beautifully adorned and joined in the *dharmamudrā* at the syllable *vaṃ*, which has the form of the rays of the autumn moon.
And thus,
because of the statement: "The syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* are not desired for the *piṇḍa* arising from the syllable," it follows that—
One should visualize the syllable *repha* within one’s own heart, from which arises a solar mandala; by that very same *hūṃ*, one should likewise manifest the essential nature of wisdom and means.
From the syllable *hūṃ*, a black and most terrible vajra arises;
one should then meditate upon the reality of *hūṃ* situated in the center of the vajra’s hub.

Having transformed all this according to the instruction, one should visualize the lunar disc. Then, having seen the terrifying Vajrin emerge from that [disc] and ascend into the sky, one should cause him to enter oneself according to the instruction to be described hereafter; thus, one becomes identical with one's own chosen deity.
And so it was said by the Blessed One in the *Mūlatantra*:
"Having visualized [the seed-syllable] transformed into the syllable *HŪṂ*, one should meditate upon oneself as the essence of Hatred.

Because of this statement, having accomplished the state of one's own chosen deity, one should emanate all the wrathful deities, intensely agitated by garlands of flames. Having seen them in their respective places, one should contemplate them as follows: one should visualize Yamāntaka, who is great black in color and holds a vajra-mallet in his right hand, in the eastern direction.

One should place Prajñāntaka, who is great white and holds a white staff, in the south. One should visualize Padmāntaka, who is great red and holds a vajra-lotus, in the principal western direction. One should contemplate Vighnāntaka, who is great blue and holds a formidable vajra, in the north on the right. One should contemplate Acalarāja, who is great black and holds a sword, in the northeast on the right. One should visualize Ṭakkirāja, who is great black and holds a goad, in the southeast at the principal position. One should look upon Nīladaṇḍa, who is great black and holds a blue staff, on the right in the southwest. One should place Mahābala, who is great black and has a trident in his hand, in the northwest at the principal position. Above, one should look upon Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, who is yellow in color and holds a wheel on the right. Below, one should contemplate Sumbharāja, who is smoke-colored and terrifying, holding a mace on the right. These wrathful deities (krodhas) are to be meditated upon as having three eyes, with tawny hair standing erect, adorned by various nāgas, possessing two arms and one face, being dwarfish with protruding bellies, and holding a vajra-noose attached to their left arms. However, among them, Ṭakkirāja and Acala are graceful and have distorted faces. Furthermore, all of them are to be visualized standing in the pratyālīḍha posture upon sun-maṇḍalas on universal lotuses.
Oṃ sumbha niḥsumbha hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ gṛhṇa 2 hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ gṛhṇāpaya 2 hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ ānaya ho bhagavan vidyārāja hūṃ 2 phaṭ |

Having thus commanded them with these and other words by means of the Vajrī, and having received that command, [the practitioner] goes there, seizes the Vināyakas, and, reflecting that they are established in their respective places, he positions the *kīla*—with its spike-point downward and its upper end upward—in the form of the King of Nectar (*amṛtarāja*), possessing a radiance filled with garlands of flames. Having commanded the Wrathful Ones through the mantra, the wise one, having received their command, should nail down the host of obstacles with this mantra.

Oṃ gha gha ghātaya 2 sarvaduṣṭān phaṭ! Kīlaya 2 sarvapāpān phaṭ! Hūṃ 3! O Vajrakīla, Vajradhara commands: nail down the vajra-body, speech, and mind of all wicked obstructors! Hūṃ phaṭ! Having thus nailed down all obstructors, one should visualize the vajra-hammer, the emblem of the King of Wrath. Reciting: "Oṃ vajramudgara vajrakīla ākoṭaya 2 hūṃ phaṭ!"—by striking with this, one becomes free of obstacles. Thereafter, one should visualize the sun in front by means of the syllable *repha*.
Upon that sun, one should visualize a universal vajra born from the syllable *hūṃ*;
with that very vajra, one should manifest a rampart and a cage-binding.

By means of this instruction to be explained hereafter within the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*), one should visualize the great protection. Having meditated on the all-pervading *dharmodaya* in its center, one should visualize within that the palace (*kūṭāgāra*) adorned with eight cremation grounds, which is the mandala of the four great elements transformed from the syllable *yaṃ* and so forth.
Therefore, he says:
"In the east stands the fierce and formidable [deity], adorned with a *śirīṣa* tree;
one should station there the famous Yakṣa Gajānana, who is Śakra."
And the serpent Vāsuki joined with a cloud adorned by thundering,
and Meru, the king of mountains— this eternal shrine shines resplendently.
Furthermore, in the south is the vessel (karaṅka) adorned with a mango tree;
there resides the renowned Yakṣa Mahiṣāsya, established as the guardian of the quarter of Yama.
There, one should join the nāga named Padma, adorned with a whirlpool of clouds,
as well as the Malaya king of mountains and the Piśuna caitya.
On the back [of the chariot] is the one named Jvālākula, adorned with *aśoka* trees;
there stands the makara-faced yakṣa, made radiant by Varuṇa.
One should visualize the serpent Karkoṭaka there as a terrible cloud;
one should then assign Mount Kailāsa as the Saṃjñā-caitya.
And in the northern region, there is a dense forest adorned with aśvattha trees;
there one should contemplate the yakṣa Narānana and Kubera.
One should apply the mind to the mental altar, visualizing the renowned serpent Takṣaka, accompanied by swirling clouds, and the Mandara mountain in its full form.
To the northeast is Lakṣmīvana, adorned with a banyan tree;
the Yakṣa Gomukha resides there and should meditate upon Maheśvara.
The nāga Śaṅkhapāla is renowned there, adorned by Caṇḍamegha;
and here too is Mount Mahendra and a non-dual caitya.
In the southeast, a *karañjaka* tree shines with a loud, boisterous laugh;
there dwells the well-known yakṣa Ajānan, adorned by fire.
Furthermore, one should visualize the great Naga Mahapadma adorned by dense clouds,
and the Gandhamadana mountain situated there as a reliquary of the body (*kāyacaitya*).
In the southwest is a place of terrible darkness, adorned with creepers and *parkaṭī* trees;
there dwells a Yakṣa with a face like a corpse, presided over by the Lord of Rākṣasas.
Furthermore, one should assign the serpent Ananta, adorned with clouds and full of rain,
as well as the golden king of mountains and the jewel stūpa.
In the northwest is the place known as Kilikilārava, filled with trees and earth-dwellers;
there resides the yakṣa Kuraṇgāsya, who has made it radiant through the Maruts.
One should assign the Kulika Nāga, the year filled with the Āgheṇa [element],
Śrīdhara, Girirāja, and Dharmacaitya.

These cremation grounds, situated within the center of the great protection wheel and interspersed with the mountains of the eight directions, are terrifying and formidable abysses filled with throngs of *vetālas* and *bhūtas*, as well as *yakṣas*, *kumbhāṇḍas*, and *rākṣasas*, crowded with snakes, tigers, bones, and garlands of skulls, and resounding with the howling of jackals.

Having reflected upon the movements [of the winds], one should visualize within that [space] a gabled pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*)—square, with four doors, adorned with four archways (*toraṇa*), beautified by eight pillars, provided with four altars (*vedikā*), graced with necklaces and half-necklaces (*hārārdhahāra*), and endowed with *pakṣinī* cornices. Having contemplated the luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), [one realizes] in terms of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*):

"Since the entire world is indeed visualized by the mind, yet nothing is visualized [ultimately], because of the thorough knowledge of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), there is no visualization at all."
By this, having seen even the entire triple world as devoid of appearance, one should recite the great king of mantras: Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness.

Thereafter, one should contemplate the sequence of the fivefold awakening (*pañcākārābhisaṃbodhi*) directed toward the focal point of the *he*-syllable vajra, starting from space. In this regard, from the transformation of the syllable *ā*, there arises the moon of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*); from the transformation of the syllable *kā*, there arises the sun of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*). The Hevajra symbol situated between these two is called the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇajñāna*). The performance of all [these] as one is the accomplishment of the image, which is pure reality (*śuddhadharmatā*). Having become unified with these, one should visualize one's own chosen deity—whether sixteen-armed, six-armed, four-armed, or two-armed—standing in a dancing posture with half-lotus position (*ardhaparyaṅka*), endowed with the six mudrās, with tawny hair standing upright, adorned with a garland of severed heads, black in color, most terrifying, bearing the singular form of the three worlds, absorbed in union with Nairātmyā, and possessed of the delight of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
Then, one should visualize the local deities through the application of the five aspects.
Therein, one should meditate on Gaurī in the east and place Caurī in the south;
Vetālī is said to be in the west, and one should arrange Ghasmarī in the northwest.

Thereafter, having placed the four goddesses beginning with Pukkasi in the corners starting from the northeast (aiśānī) in due order, one should meditate on the eight [mudrās] according to the method to be described. Bhūcarī, Khecarī, and Nairātmā are to be visualized here within one's own body, respectively, in the lotuses of body, speech, and mind, in accordance with the Root Tantra. Furthermore, this maṇḍala-circle has already been stated to be the form of the sādhya. Having accomplished one's chosen deity in the form of Hatred (Dveṣa), and having visualized the circle of ḍākinīs and caused the Gandharva-being to enter, the Vajrī, through the passion of bliss, became melted together with his consort.

Then the four goddesses, Pukkasī and the others, being deeply dejected upon seeing the absence of the Lord of the Mandala (Cakrapati), awaken their own minds once more and incite the Lord with vajra-songs. By the power of the momentum of his previous vows, the Lord too shall arise like one awakened from sleep upon hearing the vajra-song. Drawing in the moving and non-moving world with rays arising from the awakening of the bodhicitta consisting of the five gnoses, and having caused it to enter therein, he takes hold of the deities of the mandala; becoming of one flavor (*samarasībhūya*), through instruction, he should behold the innate image (*sahajabimba*)—the single form of the three worlds, the Great Peace, possessing the luster of a moonstone gem. Having thus accomplished the *anuyoga*, the Vajra-holder then performs the placement of seed-syllables (*bījanyāsa*) within the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, beginning with the Vajras and ending with the Sky-farers (*khecarī*): [he should place] the syllable *Āṃ* in Form (*rūpa*); *Iṃ* is prescribed for Feeling (*vedanā*); again, the syllable *Īṃ* in Perception (*saṃjñā*); he should place *Uṃ* in Mental Formations (*saṃskāra*); and again, the syllable *Aṃ*.

In consciousness, one should place the syllable *uṃ* by virtue of its nature as the five aggregates; in flesh, the syllable *ṛṃ*; in blood, it should again be *ṝṃ*; in the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), *ḷṃ*; and in marrow and fat, again *ḷṃ*. One should contemplate the syllable *eṃ* in the portion of form and in sound; the syllable *aiṃ* in the object of smell; the syllable *oṃ* in taste; having contemplated the syllable *auṃ* in touch, and the syllable *aṃ* from the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Having accomplished the "excessive yoga" (*atiyoga*) by this means, one should commence the "great yoga" (*mahāyoga*).

Having meditated upon four lotuses at the navel, heart, throat, and forehead, and having placed [the syllables] *aṃ*, *hūṃ*, *oṃ*, and *haṃ* there, one should contemplate the consecration of the three—body and so forth. Having meditated on the King of Syllables (*akṣararāja*) as white in color, one should emit rays of light from the head; filling the sky with a multitude of bodies [emanated] from that, and then withdrawing them, one causes them to enter back into the original seed-syllable, whereby one becomes the Body-Vajra (*kāyavajra*).
*Oṃ, all phenomena have the nature of the Holder of the Body-Vajra; I am of the nature of the Body-Vajra.*

One should meditate on the syllable ĀḤ at the path of speech; one should visualize it as red in color. Having emanated rays of light from it, and having seen the sky filled with a multitude of Speech-Vajras, one should withdraw them and contemplate them as entering back into that very same original seed-syllable. Thus one becomes a Holder of the Speech-Vajra: *Oṃ, I am the self-nature of all phenomena which are of the nature of the Speech-Vajra, whose essence is the self of the Speech-Vajra.*

One should meditate on the seed-syllable of the three worlds; one should visualize it as black in color upon the path of the mind. Having emitted rays of light from that seed-syllable and seen the sky filled with a multitude of mind-vajras, one should contemplate them dissolving back into that very [seed-syllable] and entering the sovereign seed-syllable, thereby becoming a holder of the mind-vajra.
*Oṃ, all phenomena have the nature of the mind-vajra-holder; I am the nature of the mind-vajra-holder.*
And so, in the Mantra-kula-paṭala, it was stated by the Blessed One through sound: "Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ is the consecration of body, speech, and mind"—this is my word.

Having empowered body, speech, and mind, one should meditate on the state of Hatred-Vajra. Having accomplished the Mahāyoga by means of this and having meditated according to the previously mentioned sequence, one should become the embodiment of Hatred. One should visualize oneself as black in color, extremely fierce, treading upon the four Māras, endowed with the six mudrās, and accompanied by Nairātmyā. Why is it said thus?
Because of the statement: "One should contemplate the Lord of the Mandala, arisen from the form of a sentient being."

Now, having meditated upon the colors, symbols, and so forth according to the prescribed yoga, and having recited "I am the essence of the three samayas," one should become the essence of the three samayas and begin the practice for attaining the *vidyā*. I shall describe the practice for that *vidyā* which is desired by the mind, born from the *cittavajra*, endowed with all auspicious marks, possessing wisdom, immovable, the crest-jewel of virtues, modest in this world, compassionate toward sentient beings, and filled with devotion toward the practitioner—describing it according to the appropriate application. Having meditated on the syllable *Oṃ* at the head, one should place the syllable *Hūṃ* at the heart. One should contemplate the syllable *Svā* at the navel, and the syllable *Āḥ* on the two thighs. Having placed the syllable *Kā* on the two feet, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the limbs of the Blessed Lady exactly as was done for the Blessed Lord.
Vajrā is always proclaimed to be in form; Gaurī is remembered in sensation;
Vāriyoginī is in perception; and Vajraḍākinī is in mental formations.
In the aggregate of consciousness, there is selflessness through the deposition of seeds according to reality.

One should place the seed-syllables of the four goddesses, Pukkasī and the others, within the four elements. Gaurī and the others are proclaimed to reside in the sense-bases (āyatanas) such as the eyes. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the Blessed Lady upon the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, one should perform the consecration of the lotus and the vajra. One should meditate on a lotus by means of the syllable *ĀḤ*, having the form of the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*). In its center, one should contemplate the hollow interior of the lotus bud and its filaments, born from the syllable *HŪṂ*. Following that, one should visualize a vajra produced from the syllable *HŪṂ*. One should meditate on the hollow of its jewel with the syllable *OṂ* and consecrate it with the mantra.
Oṃ! O Lotus, support of bliss, giver of the bliss of great passion, partaker of the four joys, O Viśva! Hūṃ 3! Accomplish my purpose!
Oṃ vajra, great hatred, bestower of the four joys!
O Lord whose singular essence is the face of the sky-goer, hūṃ 3, accomplish my purpose!

Thus, having empowered the lotus and vajra through this ritual yoga, one should arouse passion. Having done so externally as well, one should practice according to one's desire. This is the samādhi called Ādiyoga, which culminates in the attainment of the bliss of great rapture.

Then, having formed the ego-identification with the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) by means of that [deity], one should cause passion through the Speech-Vajra. Through meditative union (*samāpatti*), by means of the passion of great passion (*mahārāga*), one perceives the bodhicitta arising from great bliss within the interior of the lotus-receptacle. With attachment to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one stirs and brings forth the essence produced from the vajra-lotus with the gustatory faculty, and thereby satisfies oneself, until it reaches the state of being the food for all the Tathāgatas, Vajrayoginīs, Krodhas, and so forth.

Thereafter, having visualized whatever remains of the *bodhicitta*—even that which exists as a mere drop or fragment—as arising from that [semen] and consisting of the Lord together with the wheel [of deities], one should emit the *hūṃ*-vajra into the center of the Mother’s city; having brought it in through the path of Vajraḍāka and entered [the womb], one should contemplate that one should release the Blessed Lady just like water, by means of the syllable *aṃ*.

Then, one should meditate upon one’s own chosen deity, the Great Kṛṣṇa, whose tawny hair stands upright, who is endowed with the six mudrās, who has five skulls as an ornament on his head, whose topknot is bound with a garland and a silk cloth, who performs the half-lotus posture while dancing, who is naked, and who is possessed of the nine sentiments of dance.

The erotic (śṛṅgāra) 1, the heroic (vīra) 2, the loathsome (bībhatsa) 3, the furious (raudra) 4, the comic (hāsya) 5, the terrifying (bhayānaka) 6, the pathetic (karuṇā) 7, the marvelous (adbhuta) 8, and the peaceful (śānta) 9 aesthetic flavors.

One should visualize the Lord, the Blessed One, marked with a double-vajra (viśvavajra) on his crown, his face contorted with a frown, possessing three eyes, most terrifying, filled with the blazing flames of the fire of universal destruction, treading upon the four Māras, his body adorned with a garland of human heads, having the graceful form of a sixteen-year-old, and united with his consort. Just as one visualizes the Blessed One, so too should one meditate upon the Blessed Lady. Furthermore, she is endowed with the five mudrās, her body adorned with a garland of dried human heads, and her hands busily holding a flaying knife and a skull-cup. The remainder is to be understood as being like the Blessed One. In the eight skull-cups of the right hand, one should know there are, in order: an elephant, a horse, a donkey, a cow, a camel, a man, a śarabha, and a wolf. Likewise, in the eight skull-cups of the left hand, one should meditate upon Earth, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Agni, Candra, Sūrya, Yama, and Kubera. The first face is black. The left—

The [right] face is red; the right [face] is white; the upward-facing [face] is smoky and distorted; the remaining four faces are like the color of a bhrṅga bee. [This is the form] of the one with sixteen arms and four feet.

In the first left hand he holds a trident, and in the other left hand he holds a vajra-bell; in the right hands, with two arms, he holds a vajra and a flaying knife. He has three faces: the principal face is black, the left is red, and the right is extremely white. Treading upon a corpse, one should visualize him joined with Vajraśṛṅkhalā by means of his remaining two arms—thus for the six-armed form.

One should meditate on him who has one face, stands upon a corpse, and is embraced by Vajravārāhī with his remaining two arms; he holds a skull-cup in his left hand and a vajra in his right. This is for the four-armed form.

One should meditate on [the deity] as standing upon a corpse, holding a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) adorned with a digit of the moon in the left hand and a blazing vajra in the right—thus for the two-armed form.

All have their bodies adorned with the aforementioned colors and originate from the syllable *hūṃ*. For the two-armed [deities], the Wisdom Consort (*prajñā*) is Vajra; she is entirely like Nairātmyā, differing only in name. Embracing the *khaṭvāṅga* displayed at the time of walking, thus all the Blessed Lords are joined with their Wisdom Consorts and stand in the dancing posture of the half-lotus (*ardhaparyaṅka*).

Therefore, having seen oneself as the Blessed One in such a form, one should subsequently emit the circle of goddesses through the union of the churning stick and the churning vessel in one's own desired form: GAṂ CAṂ VAṂ GHAṂ PAṂ.

Having emitted [the deities] with the seed-syllables *śaṃ*, *caṃ*, and *ḍaṃ*, one should visualize Gaurī in the east—black in color, holding a knife in her right hand and a red lotus in her left, trampling upon Brahmā, and having the nature of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). In the south, one should contemplate Caurī—red in color, holding a fire-pot in her right hand and a boar in her left, trampling upon a corpse, and having the nature of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*). In the west, one should see Vettālī, holding a tortoise in her right hand and a skull-cup in her left, possessing the hue of molten gold, having the nature of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*), and mounted upon Narasiṃha. In the north, one should visualize Ghasmarī, resembling a ruby, holding a serpent in her right hand and a yogic vessel (*yogapātrikā*) in her left, mounted upon Rudra, and having the essential form of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). In the northeast, one should imagine Pukkasī—blue in color, holding a lion in her right hand and a rib in her left, mounted upon a donkey, and having the nature of the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*). In the southeast, one should create Śabarī—white in color, holding an alms-bowl in her right hand and a *khikkhirī* (a type of musical instrument) in her left, mounted upon Vittanāyaka, and having the essential nature of the water element (*abdhātu*). In the southwest, one should establish Caṇḍālī, who has the luster of the sky, holding a discus in her right hand and a plow in her left, seated upon a Rākṣasa, and having the nature of the fire element (*tejodhātu*). In the northwest, the knower of yoga should contemplate Ḍombinī, who is multicolored, holding a blazing vajra in her right hand and a threatening gesture (*tarjanikā*) in her left, mounted upon Vemacitrin, and having the nature of the wind element (*vāyudhātu*). Furthermore, Bhūcarī, Khecarī, and Nairātmā should be meditated upon as having entered through the emission and re-absorption of the Lord, each in their respective previously mentioned locations according to order.

All these [deities] should be visualized as having three eyes, with tawny hair standing erect, endowed with the five mudrās, naked, in a dancing posture with one leg half-bent, fierce in appearance, sixteen years of age, and seated upon moon-discs.

Having thus produced the wheel, the Vajrin situated in its center perceives the infinite world-realms filled with networks of light rays radiating from his own body. Having visualized himself in their midst as an illusory emanation, he sends forth networks of light rays from the seed-syllable at his heart, which travel through the boundless and limitless sky, bringing back the wisdom-wheel identical to his own commitment-wheel. Having beheld it before him and offered the water for the feet, the guest-offering, and so forth, he causes it to enter his own commitment-wheel in due order and should transform it into the form of the glorious syllable *HĒ*.

Thereafter, at the time of unification, having seen all the Tathāgatas, Vajrayoginīs, Bodhisattvas, Krodhas, and so forth, emerging from the rays of light issuing from one’s own body, one should request empowerment, saying: "May all the Tathāgatas empower me! Then, by those five Tathāgatas:
"Just as all the Tathāgatas were bathed immediately upon birth, so shall I bathe you with pure divine water."
Oṃ, for the glory of the commitment of the empowerment of all Tathāgatas, hūṃ!

By this, they are consecrated. The Vajra-Ḍākinīs raise shouts of "Victory! Victory! The Bodhisattvas, being well-pleased, behold themselves. The Wrathful Deities and others address them from the sky. A tumultuous clamor of various musical sounds arises. One should contemplate that saffron, sandalwood, gold, and other jewels rain down; then, the Lord of the Mind (Cittesha) should be placed upon the head of both [the practitioner and] the Bhagavatī. Gaurī and the others are sealed by Cittesha, Śāśvata, Ratnesha, and Amitābha—[namely] Hatred...
One should mark the heads of the Pukkasīs and others with the pigments of delusion, greed, and passion; then, with delighted minds, Locanā and the other goddesses praise him with song.
You were surrounded by a host of yoginīs, yet you were won over by your own mind. By you, with a heart of compassion, that Śāla tree was adorned and awakened;
you performed this deed within the illusion of Māyā. O King of Śrī-Heruka, may your mind be satisfied!

Then, in the midst of the assembly of vidyās, the Vajrī endowed with wisdom produces the nectar of food. One should meditate on a blue wind-wheel in the shape of a bow produced from the syllable *yaṃ*; above that, a red fire in the shape of a triangle produced from the seed-syllable of the sun; and above that, within the three syllables, one should meditate on a lotus vessel containing three severed heads, situated below which is the vessel. Furthermore, the vessel is empowered by the syllable *āḥ*. Having meditated on the mantra beginning with *buṃ*, one should consider the syllable *oṃ* to be above that, and contemplate *hūṃ* above it. Having liquefied [the substances] with this fire of meditation, one should visualize the five nectars and five lamps in the form of mercury. By the rays of the syllable *hūṃ*, one pleases the infinite and boundless Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, brings forth the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*), and unifies them. Stirring it with the *hūṃ*-born vajra, the vajra melts and dissolves into the nectar. One should see it as extremely cool, having been kindled by the syllable *oṃ* and awakened by the syllable *āḥ*. Thereafter, using the ladle of one's arm, one draws up the nectar with the three syllables and offers it into the belly of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍodara*). One should meditate on the deities of the maṇḍala in the same manner.

Then, having meditated upon the Blessed One in the midst of the eight cremation grounds, with a body that radiates and reabsorbs [light], and having disciplined those to be trained by means of this, one should contemplate him as dissolved right there. This is the samādhi called "The Supreme King of Mandalas."
First, one should meditate on the black [form] according to the appropriate application;
having meditated upon the six limbs, one should subsequently relinquish the color.

After meditating on the subtle yoga that will be described immediately following the six limbs, there is the dismissal (*visarjana*). The mantra-practitioner should contemplate the clear light (*prabhāsvara*) as being the very nature of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). One should dissolve the beings of the maṇḍala; having grasped the sphere of the aggregates, one should then understand that Gaurī and the others have emerged from the bodhicitta.

Gaurī is in the form of the Blessed One, Caurī has gone into feeling (*vedanā*), Vettālī is in the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā*), and Ghasmarī is in the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra*).
The earth is Caṇḍālī; among them, Ḍombinī resides in the wind.

Having withdrawn the assembly of the *ḍākinī* host according to the instruction, one should thereafter contemplate oneself as the supreme state of clear light (*prabhāsvara*). Having realized Nairātmyā within consciousness, one should again emanate seed-syllables and rays of light. By means of that, having unified [them], the Blessed One remains in the state of his own seed-syllable. Thereafter, having meditated upon the moon, sun, and seed-syllables as having become one—a mass of blazing rays—this gradually becomes like the flame of a lamp. Thereafter, one should meditate on it as having the singular form of the core of a plantain tree until non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) occurs. For this very reason:
There is neither beginning, nor end, nor middle; there is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa. This is that supreme great bliss—neither other nor self.
Having entered the state of luminosity, one should contemplate the arising;
by means of the yoga of instantaneous form, one should visualize the Lord of the Wheel.
However, it has been taught by the practitioner, the Great Sage Śākya, that one should meditate upon the manifestation of the being-form exactly according to the sequential instruction.

Now, the mantra recitation (*jāpa*), the offering (*bali*), the reality (*tattva*), and the subtle yoga (*sūkṣmayoga*) are introduced. The mantra syllables, having emerged from the mouth of the Bhagavatī accompanied by rays of light, enter one’s own mouth; proceeding via the path of the *avadhūtī*, they enter the lotus of the Bhagavatī through the *vajra* path. Then, the mantra syllables [emerge] again from the mouth of the Bhagavatī into one’s own mouth. Following this sequence, one should perform the recitation according to the application of colors for rites such as pacification (*śāntika*) until exhaustion. This is the *dolājāpa*. One should visualize the mantra syllables seated in the form of a mandala upon the sun at the heart, with their heads pointing upward. This is the *piṇḍajāpa*. All the mantra syllables are uttered with a long resonance (*dīrghanāda*). This is the *samayajāpa*. Furthermore, the recitation should be performed according to the instruction on the Great Heart-mantra (*mahaddhṛdaya*).
One should always meditate upon the Vajra-holder, who possesses the form of primordial wisdom, as inconceivable.
Oṃ deva picuvajra hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | [This is] for the sixteen-armed [deity].
Oṃ trailokyākṣepa hūṃ 3 phaṭ svāhā. [This is] for the two-armed [form].
Oṃ jvala-jvalābhyāṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. [This is] for the four-armed one.
Oṃ kiṭi 2 vajra hūṃ 3 phaṭ svāhā | [This is] for the six-armed [deity].
This is the heart-mantra of all. Furthermore, the near-heart-mantra is:
Oṃ vajrakartari hevajrāya hūṃ 3 phaṭ svāhā.

Oṃ! To the eight-faced one, whose tawny hair and eyebrows stand erect, who has twenty-four eyes and sixteen arms, whose body is like a dark cloud, who wears various garlands of skulls, whose heart is swollen with cruelty, and who has fangs like a half-moon: slay, slay! Cause [them] to be slain, cause [them] to be slain! Roar, roar! Threaten, threaten! Dry up, dry up the seven oceans! Bind, bind the eight nāgas! Seize, seize all enemies! Ha hā hi hī hu hū he hai ho hau haṃ haḥ phaṭ svāhā! This is the root mantra of the Blessed One.
Oṃ, to the eight-faced one, hūṃ 2 phaṭ! Oṃ, to him whose tawny hair stands upright in matted locks, hūṃ 2 phaṭ!

Oṃ, to the twenty-four-eyed one, hūṃ 2 phaṭ! Oṃ, to the sixteen-armed one, hūṃ 2 phaṭ! Oṃ, to him whose body is like a dark rain-cloud, hūṃ 2 phaṭ! Oṃ, to the bearer of many garlands of skulls, hūṃ 2 phaṭ! Oṃ, to him whose mind is fierce and inflated with wrath, hūṃ 2 phaṭ! Oṃ, to him who has fangs like a half-moon, hūṃ 2 phaṭ!
The eight-syllable mantra of the Blessed One.
Oṃ aṃ nairātmye hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ vajraḍākinīye aṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | These are the heart and near-heart mantras.
Oṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ phaṭ svāhā.
This is the root mantra of the Bhagavatī.

Oṃ aṃ āṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ iṃ īṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ uṃ ūṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ lṃ ḷṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ eṃ aiṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ oṃ auṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ aṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ | This is the eight-syllable mantra of the Bhagavatī.
Oṃ gaṃ vajragaurīyai hūṃ 2 phaṭ.
Oṃ caṃ vajracauryai hūṃ 2 phaṭ.
Oṃ vaṃ, to Vajravetālī, hūṃ 2 phaṭ!
Oṃ ghaṃ vajraghasmarīyai hūṃ 2 phaṭ.
Oṃ puṃ vajrapukkasīyai hūṃ 2 phaṭ.
Oṃ śaṃ vajraśabarīye hūṃ 2 phaṭ.
Oṃ caṃ vajracaṇḍālyai hūṃ 2 phaṭ.
Oṃ ḍaṃ vajraḍombinyai hūṃ 2 phaṭ.

In this way, one should recite the mantra according to one's desire by means of the previously mentioned procedure. However, in the midst of that, one should also recite the root mantra of the Blessed One; and at the time of praise, one should perform the praise with the verses of the Tathāgatas.

Thereafter, having stood in the state of Dveṣavajra through the sequence of the samādhi of the Vajra of the Light of Gnosis, and having understood the wrathful deities according to their respective forms, he summons the obstructors (vināyakas) residing in the three realms: Oṃ inda jama jala jakkha bhuda vahni vāu rakkha | canda sujja mada bappa talapātāla addhasappa sāhā ||

Having consecrated [the offerings] with this mantra and caused them to enter the three cities of Great Liberation, one should generate the void according to the previously mentioned sequence. Having produced those [deities] by means of the three syllables and empowered them in the form of body, speech, and mind, one should visualize oneself in the form of their arms and faces. At the time of offering the oblation of flowers, incense, perfumes, and so forth, the mantra-holder who wields the vajra and bell should sing the song of the supreme commitment (*paramasamayagītikā*) in a low, warbling tone (*kākalikayā*), for the purpose of bringing about the presence of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*), according to the oral instructions. Immediately thereafter: "Consume this oblation! Smell it! Enjoy the flowers and incense! Taste the meat!"
Accomplish all our tasks; indeed, remove the knot of anger.
With this [verse], one should present the offering of oblations; one should cause them to consume it and satisfy oneself as well.

Oṃ, the syllable *a* is the gateway to all phenomena because they are primordially unarisen. Oṃ āḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Having satisfied [the deity] with this and having praised [them] with the root mantra, one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra. Thereafter, having dismissed [the deity] three times with "Oṃ vajra muḥ," the Twilight Song (*saṃdhyāgītā*) should be sung once more. By this, the meditative absorption named "Supreme King of Rituals" (*karmarājāgrī*) is accomplished.

Then, when one is seized by wind due to the power of [past] cultivation, at that time, for the sake of its remedy, one should first say: having meditated on the moon of the syllable *oṃ* at the head, one should visualize oneself being nourished by a great rain of nectar until health is attained.

Then, having contemplated one’s own emblem within the *dharma*, and having visualized the Universal Monarch together with his wheel in the lotus at its center, one should determine there the size of the emblem to be merely as thick as a mustard seed. Thus, regarding the Lord of Samādhi here as the Master whose very nature is the wheel, one should always become subtler than the subtle. When the mind is fixed there and becomes certainly stable, one should constantly manifest the Lord of the Wheel; he shall be filled with the network of the *ḍākinīs* and the *kula*s. One should perceive the sky filled [with him], the inconceivability of all phenomena. Immediately following this, I shall explain the two types of armor through the grace of the Tree of Dharma.
Akṣobhya is in the form of the wheel, Amitābha is the nature of the earrings;
Ratneśa is in the necklace around the neck, and Vairocana resides in the hand. Amoghasiddhi is situated in the girdle, and one should perceive the Holder of the Vajra (Vajradhara) in all the limbs.
Mohavajrī resides in the eyes; Dveṣavajrikā in the two ears;
Mātsaryakī is said to be in the nose; Rāgavajrikā in the mouth;
Īrṣyāvajrī in the body; and Nairātmyayoginī is in the mind.

Having understood this meaning according to the instruction and having donned the great armor, the yogi should seize [the essence] from within the house of the three worlds through the yoga of Sahaja-Hevajra.

This conclusion, which was guarded with effort by the venerable Rāhula—the teacher of my feet and the teacher of teachers—will become the very essence of the minds of all beings; for it has been said that truth alone remains.
Therefore, I have diligently clarified this sequence for the sake of the bliss of realization.
May those who have faith in the system of the Yoginīs rejoice in the bliss called Bhadra.
Thus.
The *Dveṣavajrasādhana* is completed. This work is the composition of the accomplished master, the venerable Bhadrapāda.
